questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral as a Repeated Integral Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem: Consider the closed curve $C,$ which is the boundary of the region enclosed by $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and the $x$-axis, for $\pi \le x\le 2\pi .$ Express ${\int }_{C}xdx-(x-y)dy$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066044/assets/264cb888010525848f647669653d34383535dd32e6ac264927105540c3b85f9f.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=x$ and $Q(x,y)=-(x-y).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=0,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):\pi \le x\le 2\pi ,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡x\le y\le 0}
$$

Therefore, applying the Green's Theorem we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xdx-(x-y)dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }{\int }_{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}^{0}dy\,dx.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem:
Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,2),(1,0)$ and $(2,0),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})\,dx+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066044/assets/8e3efc3f9c58fb0f9a84144e97a300b6ab2a4011d47ee0d2bae1edc8a3f721cd.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})$ and $Q(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}).$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{y}{x})\,dx+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=\frac{x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨{e}^{x}-{y}^{2},{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the square with vertices at $(-1,-1),$ $(1,-1),$ $(1,1)$ and $(-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066044/assets/574172dda3031b9bb44dbcfb46265453ae543a75bccf8db24e93625e7154bba9.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{y}+{x}^{2})\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{x}-{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+{x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-{y}^{2})\,dx+({e}^{y}+{x}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{[2xy+{y}^{2}]}_{-1}^{1}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}(2x(1)+(1)^{2}-2x(-1)-(-1)^{2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}4x\,dx \\  & =2{[{x}^{2}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2[(1)^{2}-(-1)^{2}] \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Line Integrals Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$ where $F(x,y)=⟨2x+{y}^{2},{x}^{2}+2y⟩$ and $C$ is the boundary of the region enclosed by the curve $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}$ and the lines $y=0$ and $x=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066044/assets/fafd281fc63fb276c9759fd84f722096d494aa3e3fe9441f43aa6ecd1f9dfda9.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(2x+{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=2x+{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+2y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le \frac{{x}^{2}}{3}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2x+{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+2y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}/3}(2x-2y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[2xy-{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{{x}^{2}/3}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{9})dx \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{4}}{6}-\frac{{x}^{5}}{45}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{(3)^{4}}{6}-\frac{(3)^{5}}{45} \\  & =\frac{27}{2}-\frac{27}{5} \\  & =\frac{81}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral as a Repeated Integral Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem: Consider the closed curve $C,$ which is the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $x=y$ and $x=4y-{y}^{2}.$ Express ${∮}_{C}({e}^{y}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dx+(2x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dy$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066044/assets/239867aec8cff7840667d2f4eafa9bc97d4fc5af09b684d863fef06fd8fd28ad.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{y}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=2x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}={e}^{y}+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2{e}^{y}+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):y\le x\le 4y-{y}^{2},\,0\le y\le 3}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{y}-2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dx+(2x{e}^{y}+{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{e}^{y}+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{e}^{y}-2x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{y}^{4y-{y}^{2}}{e}^{y}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$
